title: Kunti's mantra
hookLine: in the forest, Kunti tells Pandu about a mantra a sage gave her as a girl, and three gods answer
carry: a mantra: sacred words that call the divine
tomorrow: the cousins grow up under one roof, and something else grows with them.

cards: Years before any of this, a girl named Kunti served a sage in her father's house. He was Durvasa, hard to please, and she served him so carefully that, when he left, he gave her a gift: a mantra.
With it she could call any god she chose, and have a son by him. She has kept it quiet ever since. Now her husband sits in the forest, cursed, asking how his line can go on.

teach.b: Pandu raises it first. He tells Kunti of the old custom, the one that brought him into the world, and asks her to have sons for him. Kunti answers with her secret: the mantra.
Pandu is overjoyed. Which god first?
He chooses Dharma, so the eldest will be just. Kunti speaks the mantra, Dharma comes, and Yudhishthira is born. Next, strength: she calls Vayu, the wind, and Bhima is born.
As a baby he tumbles from her lap onto a mountain, and it's the rock that shatters. Then Indra, king of the gods, and Arjuna is born. Justice, strength and skill.
Notice how the mantra came to her: not bought, not stolen. Given by a sage, for her service, and kept quiet for years. That's how Hindus treat mantras.
Many Hindus understand a mantra as sacred sound, words that carry the presence of the one they name, which is why you hear them at pujas, weddings and morning prayers.
In many families and lineages, a personal mantra is received from a teacher and kept private, said with care, never shown off.
Many Hindus repeat one daily on a mala of a hundred and eight beads, a practice called japa. In the story, Kunti's words call a god and he comes.
In daily practice the tradition says something gentler: say the name with your whole attention, and you turn toward the one you're calling.
And notice what Kunti doesn't tell Pandu: what happened the first time she tried it. That waits a few days.

how: Many Hindus receive a mantra from a guru or an elder and repeat it daily in japa, often on a mala of 108 beads. In this story, Dharma, Vayu and Indra become fathers of the Pandava brothers.

games.q: a friend sees your grandmother whispering over a string of beads and asks if it's a spell. what fits Kunti's story best?
o: it's japa: she's repeating a mantra, sacred words that turn her toward God.
yes, mantras are magic words that make things happen on command.
it's just a habit; the words don't mean anything.
games.why: Kunti's mantra was a gift from a sage, kept with care. Hindus repeat mantras in japa to turn toward the divine, not as a trick.

practice: Try a little japa. Choose a sacred word you know: Om, or a name like Rama, Krishna or Shiva. Say it slowly eleven times, softly or in your head, counting on your fingers and giving each one your whole attention.
If you don't pray, use Om simply as a sound, and listen to it fade.

wordCard.voice: Mantra, sacred sound: Kunti's, given by Durvasa, called Dharma, Vayu and Indra to father Yudhishthira, Bhima and Arjuna.

orig.note: Sanskrit mantra: a sacred formula; Kunti's, from Durvasa, calls a god to give her a son.
